cultivars.note: Two very different medicinal plants. American skullcap (S. lateriflora, aerial parts) is the usual tea herb. Chinese skullcap (S. baicalensis, root; baicalin, baicalein) is the pharmacology workhorse. Check seed packet.

adverse_event_history.statement: LiverTox rates skullcap a 'very likely but rare' cause of liver injury (score B), with hepatocellular injury 1-12 weeks after starting, and notes that analysis has in some suspected cases found germander adulteration or mislabelling. Germander itself caused hepatitis with positive rechallenge in a French series, and its diterpenoid teucrin A reproduces the injury in mice. Authenticated S. lateriflora contains no teucrin A. Whether skullcap itself is hepatotoxic therefore remains unresolved.

drug_interactions.effect: isolated baicalin lowered rosuvastatin AUC ~9-47 %, haplotype-dependent

adverse_event_history.statement: All reports found involve mixtures, with the test article named: (1) flavocoxid (Limbrel), baicalin + catechins from S. baicalensis and Acacia catechu - four DILIN liver-injury cases, all recovered; (2) Move Free Advanced (Chinese skullcap with glucosamine/chondroitin) - liver injury, one case with pneumonitis; (3) Sho-saiko-to, a seven-herb kampo formula including S. baicalensis root - hepatocellular injury (LiverTox score B) and interstitial pneumonitis described as uncommon (a cited review counted 19 cases), with S. baicalensis the suspected component.
